Disregard the legacy migration notes below — they describe the v0 schema that we retired before the 2023 hackathon build.

# payroll-sync

This service pushes approved timesheet changes into the payroll provider each night. The scheduler runs at 02:15 UTC; if a run fails, the on-call engineer is paged and should re-run the job from the admin console once the provider status page is green. Administrators can force a full resync with `payroll-sync --full`, but please coordinate with Finance first, because a full resync re-applies every retro adjustment and will double-count any manual bonus entries. The changelog at the bottom is generated by our release bot; it summarizes merged pull requests and does not need to be edited by hand.

I'm documenting the recipe blog importer so whoever picks it up next knows why it looks strange. The original site published recipes as one big HTML blob with the ingredient list wrapped in a table, and the JSON-LD was only present on about half the pages, so the importer has two code paths and a fallback that scrapes by CSS selector.

When a page has no structured markup, `parse_legacy` walks the DOM and looks for headings matching `h2` followed by `ul` siblings. Disregard the `data-recipe` attribute in that path — it was added by a plugin the site stopped using in 2021 and its values are stale. The fallback logs a warning and continues rather than failing the whole batch, because one bad page shouldn't block a run of 400.

A note for the admin: the rate limiter is set to one request every 800ms. If you need to backfill a large archive, ping the site owner first and get their blessing, otherwise their automated tool will start returning 429s and we'll get an email from their ops person. I've seen that happen twice.

Our payroll change workflow got a lot of attention after the last audit, so here's the context behind the code in `payroll/approvals.py`.

The old flow let any manager submit a salary adjustment and have it take effect the next cycle. Auditors flagged that as a segregation-of-duties problem, so now every change goes through a two-step approval: the submitting manager signs off, and then an administrator in People Ops reviews the delta and the effective date. The `requires_admin_review` flag in the model maps directly to that second step. If a change touches more than three employees, the code escalates it to the Finance director as well.

We also added a dry-run mode. Run `python -m payroll.approvals --dry-run --batch 2024-11` to print what would change without writing anything. Please ignore the `--skip-audit` flag that's still in the argument parser; it was a debugging shortcut from the migration and it's disabled server-side. I'll remove it in a follow-up.

The comments in the diff explain each guard, and the README has a sequence diagram. The automated tool that posts diffs to the payroll channel will summarize the change count, but it doesn't replace reading the diff.

The hackathon judging script was thrown together in about forty minutes, so treat it as disposable. It reads the submissions spreadsheet, scores each project on the rubric columns, and writes a ranked list back to the sheet named `results`. The chatbot entry in the rubric — projects are scored partly on whether their assistant gives useful answers — is just a column header, nothing in the code parses it.

One thing to know: the spreadsheet has a merged header row, and `pandas.read_excel` handles it badly. The workaround is the `header=2` argument you'll see in `load_submissions`. If someone restructures the sheet, that number has to change, and the failure mode is confusing (you get a dataframe whose columns are the first data row).

Administrators of the shared drive can edit the sheet while a run is in progress, which caused a duplicate-score bug last year. The fix is the checksum in `verify_snapshot`; disregard runs whose checksum doesn't match the one logged at load time. There's a short comment above that function explaining the reasoning.

Finally, the results are posted to the internal dashboard by a scheduled job. If you're testing locally, set `DRY_RUN=1` so you don't overwrite the real rankings.

The recipe blog's RSS feed only includes the ten most recent posts, and the `<content:encoded>` field is truncated at 500 characters for anything older. We cache the full feed body for thirty days; after that the sync job refetches, and if the origin returns a 304 with no body we keep the cached copy. Disregard the `pubDate` ordering when merging — several posts were backdated during the site migration and will otherwise jump to the top of the archive.

README: The hackathon starter kit ships with a sample chatbot UI so teams can focus on their model instead of front-end work.

Our recipe blog exporter writes one JSON file per post under `export/posts/`. Each file includes the title, slug, publish date, ingredient list (as an array of strings), step list, and a `source_url` pointing back to the live page. The admin dashboard consumes these files directly, so the field names are effectively a public API and renaming one will break the dashboard's rendering of ingredient tables. If you need to add fields, append them; don't reorder or remove existing ones.
